enNames: Electric blue morph of blue acara

viNames.name: Cá phượng hoàng blue acara (Electric Blue Acara)

origin.fact: It is a colour form of the blue acara bred in captivity, not a separate wild population.
Breeders kept picking the bluest fish and bred them over many generations until the colour was strong and stable.
The electric blue colour showed up after many generations of captive breeding. No breeder or date is named.
A forum moderator called it a 'designer fish' that appeared about 10 to 12 years before his post.
A German exporter says the 'Neon Blue' breeding form is the one most kept today. It adds that the origin of the old imported ancestor stock can no longer be traced.
The wild parent species is native to Trinidad and Venezuela.
The wild blue acara lives in Venezuela and Colombia, including the Orinoco basin.

looks.fact: The whole body and fins are a bright, shining blue, much stronger than the blue-grey of wild fish.
Wild-type blue acaras have blue-grey scales. Males are brighter than females, especially when breeding.
Males are usually larger, with longer fins and deeper colour than females.
Electric blues are often a little smaller than standard blue acaras.
Forum keepers dispute that electric blues stay small, reporting fish of about 16.5 to 20 cm.

keeping.fact: Tank of at least 100 L, or 120 L or more for a pair. Use rocks, driftwood, sand or fine gravel and a few plants.
At least 40 US gallons (about 150 L), 55 gallons or more preferred. Give open swimming space and moderate light.
At least 30 gallons (about 115 L) for a pair, with sand and hiding places. It digs, so tie plants to wood or rock.
Because it is so long established in captivity, exact pH and hardness matter little.
Feed twice a day: sinking and colour pellets, artemia, worms and chopped shrimp, plus mashed boiled vegetables once or twice a week.
Eats meaty flakes or pellets, and also takes frozen and live food.
Keep with fish too big to swallow, such as medium to large South American tetras, Corydoras, plecos and peaceful cichlids like flag and keyhole cichlids.
Not safe with dwarf shrimp or small invertebrates. Large snails may be fine in a big tank.
Calm and not quarrelsome, but somewhat territorial when breeding.
Some keepers found the electric blue calmer than the regular blue acara.

breeding.fact: It lays eggs on a flat stone, and both parents guard the eggs and fry. Eggs hatch in about 2 to 3 days.
A good first breeding cichlid. A well-fed pair claims a territory. Fry use their yolk for a few days, then take crushed flakes, micro-worms or vinegar eels.
The parents often move the fry into pits dug in the substrate. Electric blues can be harder to breed reliably than wild-type fish.
It breeds true: offspring keep the electric blue colour.

health.fact: Slightly more delicate than the standard blue acara, possibly because of selective breeding. It does best in a stable, well-kept tank.
A moderator found it hardier than electric blue Jack Dempseys, which are weaker than their normal form.
Not hard to keep healthy in captivity.

buying.fact: Buy from sellers known for healthy stock. Electric blues sell for more than standard blue acaras.
A Vietnamese shop sells 6 to 7 cm fish. Pick males for size, longer fins and stronger colour.

controversy.fact: A US retailer calls it a hybrid and says many think it was made by crossing with the blue ram, then line-bred. It also admits the origin is debated.
Another retailer says plainly that it is not a hybrid with another species and is not dyed.
A German exporter says it is unclear whether trade blue acaras are truly A. pulcher or a close relative.
Some sources get the basic facts wrong: one article calls this South American species a Central American cichlid.
